title: Bypassing the bottleneck: broad-host geminivirus enables systemic, tissue-culture-free plant genome editing
content: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna were awarded the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their groundbreaking discovery of the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing method. Since this discovery, there have been many advancements of CRISPR-Cas technologies that have revolutionized plant functional genomics and crop improvement. However, utilizing these powerful molecular tools across diverse plant species has been bottlenecked by traditional genetic transformation methods. Standard Agrobacterium-mediated transformation or biolistic (gene gun) delivery methods depend on labor-intensive tissue culture and regeneration processes that are often restricted to specific plant species/genotypes. These delivery methods release the plasmids containing CRISPR machinery in the isolated cells/tissue explants/protoplasts, and the sequence encoding the guide RNA (gRNA) promoter, gRNA, and Cas protein is integrated into the genome. Using the specialized combinations of plant hormones, antibiotics, and tissue culture, these cells are forced to multiply and regenerate into transformed adult plants. For many crops, especially recalcitrant cultivars, this regeneration step is slower and more genotype dependent than the DNA editing reaction itself. Thus, delivery and regeneration, rather than the CRISPR chemistry, remain major bottlenecks for broad genome editing in plants (Baltes et al 2014; Steinberger and Voytas 2025).
